title: Epsilon Systems - Discovery: Migration from OpenAI to Dedicated
summary: Initial discovery focused on feasibility and constraints for migrating from OpenAI hosted to Redwood Dedicated/private deployment. Key concerns: API compatibility, eval parity, latency vs cost, data residency and KMS integration. Agreed to run eval parity tests and a small benchmark pilot on Dedicated nodes.
action_items: Maya Patel: Send security pack (SOC2 report, ISO certs, network diagram) — due 2026-11-05
Diego Suarez: Share recommended Dedicated sizing and cost estimate + throughput numbers for 8k/16k seq — due 2026-11-06
Leah Kim: Provide representative prompt set and evaluation criteria for parity tests — due 2026-11-04
next_steps: Redwood to run eval parity on customer's prompt set (OpenAI vs Redwood Dedicated) and share results
Schedule technical pilot week where Redwood will run a small workload on Dedicated nodes with telemetry
Send pricing/commit options and Dedicated sizing recommendation
Customer to confirm stakeholders for procurement and security review (legal + infra)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. Diego who handles the infra side is with me. Quick intros?
[00:09] Samir: Hey this is Samir, CTO at Epsilon. Leah and Carlos are here too. Main reason is we're hitting cost and rate limits on OpenAI for some internal products, and want to explore dedicated infra.
[00:19] Diego: Great, can you give a quick snapshot of current usage, models, sequence lengths?
[00:24] Leah: Sure, we're on gpt-4-ish family endpoints via OpenAI; about 250k tokens/day, peak concurrency ~40 reqs, average seq around 2k but for some analysis flows we spike to 8k-12k. We also run retrieval augmented generation with embeddings.
[00:40] Carlos: We use a mix of embeddings + rerank then generation. Latency matters for interactive parts, batch can be slower.
[00:48] Maya: Understood. Primary asks from Redwood are hosted vs dedicated vs private? What's the driver — cost, data residency, throughput?
[00:55] Samir: It's all three. Cost predictability is huge, and also we have IP concerns so want tighter isolation. We're also evaluating private deployment options for a subset of high-sensitivity workloads.
[01:05] Diego: Two clarifying Qs: do you run any self-hosted runtime like vLLM or TGI internally today? And are you expecting 1:1 API compatibility with OpenAI?
[01:13] Leah: We have a small infra team that experimented with vLLM last quarter but it wasn't productionized. We use TGI in some PoCs. For compatibility, we want the prompts/evals to behave the same — minimal drift.
[01:23] Diego: Ok so parity is critical. On that front Redwood does two things: we support OpenAI-compatible endpoints for many models and we do model variant matching + config mapping so prompts behave similarly. Also we recommend parity tests with your prompt set.
[01:36] Samir: How frequent are issues with tokenization differences or subtle scoring differences?
[01:40] Diego: It happens — especially when switching runtimes or quantization profiles. Tokenizer difference is usually minor but can change few-shot prompts. We log and diff outputs and then tune system prompts or recommend different quantization or a slightly different model checkpoint.
[01:52] Leah: We care about embeddings too. Are your embeddings identical to OpenAI's? We've calibrated models for semantic search.
[01:58] Maya: Great question. Embedding parity is trickier; Redwood provides curated open model variants and we run embedding evals — most customers find equivalent vectors within expected drift, but we will run similarity metrics (cosine) on your dataset.
[02:12] Carlos: On infra — for Dedicated, what's the typical cluster size and can we burst to hosted if we need extra capacity?
[02:18] Diego: Yes. Dedicated is reserved GPU pools. Typical starting commit is 4 GPUs for medium workloads, we can recommend exact SKU based on your 99p latency and throughput targets. We also have burst routing to hosted as a policy for emergencies, and automatic fallbacks to smaller quantized variants.
[02:31] Samir: We did a POC with vLLM and saw memory pressure at long seqs. How does Redwood handle KV cache and long context?
[02:37] Diego: Our runtime has optimized KV cache management and attention kernels for long contexts; we also support quantization-friendly paths but we usually recommend mixed precision and specific kernels for >8k. For extreme long context we advise model variants trained for long context.
[02:51] Leah: What about throughput vs latency trade-offs — batching will help cost, but we can't add 500ms of latency on the UI.
[02:58] Diego: Right — we do continuous batching and dynamic batch sizing aware of latency SLOs. For interactive endpoints we run smaller batches and use prefix caching to reduce per-token compute. For background jobs we batch aggressively to save cost.
[03:12] Maya: On security, Carlos, can you describe your compliance needs?
[03:16] Carlos: SOC2 is required, encryption at rest and KMS integration, audit logs for all calls, SSO/SAML, and we prefer HSM support for keys. Also network isolation — VPC peering or private link.
[03:27] Maya: Redwood Dedicated and Private support KMS integrations, customer-controlled keys, audit logs, RBAC and SAML SSO. For private deployment we can do a customer-controlled control plane with VPC connectors or an on-prem bundle for air-gapped workloads. We'll share the security pack.
[03:41] Samir: Good. On migration effort — our infra team wants to know if we keep the same request/response shapes and webhooks.
[03:48] Diego: We expose OpenAI-compatible REST endpoints with additional features. In many cases you can point existing clients to Redwood with minimal code change. For model rollouts we have canary/A-B and meta headers so you can trace.
[03:59] Leah: You mentioned quantization earlier — does that change output quality for us? We use few-shot examples a lot.
[04:04] Diego: Depends on model and quant profile. 8-bit quant is often fine for many workloads but for sensitive few-shot tasks we test parity. We'll run your prompts across float32, 8-bit, and some 4-bit configs and show delta metrics.
[04:18] Samir: What about speed compared to OpenAI? Our users like sub-300ms token latency for short prompts.
[04:24] Diego: On Dedicated with appropriate GPUs and short prompt workload, we can meet sub-300 token latencies; for long seqs latency is higher but still comparable. We include tail percentiles in our SLOs and can share benchmarks.
[04:36] Maya: Let's talk procurement and timeline. Are you looking to pilot within next month?
[04:40] Samir: Ideally yes. We want a 2-week pilot to validate parity and latency. Then procurement, likely a commit for Dedicated.
[04:47] Maya: Great. We'll scope a 2-week pilot: Redwood sets up Dedicated pool, we run your prompt/eval set, capture telemetry, and iterate. Post-pilot we'll deliver a TCO and commit options.
[04:58] Carlos: For the pilot can you run a mixed workload including embeddings/rerank and gen?
[05:02] Diego: Absolutely. We'll provision GPU nodes that can handle both. We may split embedding pods and generation pods to optimize.
[05:09] Leah: I can share a 200-prompt evaluation set and a sample of stored documents for retrieval tests.
[05:14] Maya: Perfect. If you can send that today or tomorrow we'll queue the parity tests.
[05:19] Samir: One more — are there customers who've migrated from OpenAI to Redwood Dedicated with similar needs?
[05:24] Maya: Yes, a few enterprise customers in fintech and healthcare. We can share anonymized results and a short case study.
[05:30] Diego: Also note differences when customers move from vLLM self-host to Redwood: we often smooth out kernel selection and memory management so throughput improves at scale. But there can be subtle prompt-level drift; hence the parity tests.
[05:39] Leah: Good to hear. On embeddings drift, what threshold do you consider acceptable? We typically flagged drop when retrieval MRR decreases >2-3%.
[05:47] Diego: We use cosine similarity and downstream retrieval metrics; we typically aim for <2% MRR delta. If more, we either recommend a different checkpoint or fine-tune/configure prompts.
[05:57] Maya: Ok summarizing next steps: Redwood will send security docs and sizing, run parity on the prompt set Leah provides, and propose pilot dates. Customer will loop in procurement/legal. Anything else?
[06:07] Samir: No, that's it. Thanks everyone.
[06:10] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with the security pack and pilot schedule.
[06:14] [call ends]
